newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Russia, U.S. called to ratify chemical weapons ban.
newsitem.headline: Russia, U.S. called to ratify chemical weapons ban.

text.p: The United States and Russia must ratify the landmark Chemical Weapons Convention without delay, the chairman of the Hague-based commission overseeing the accord said on Friday.

"I strongly hope these two states...would confirm their long standing commitment to chemical disarmament by completing their ratification procedures between now and the entry into force of the convention," Marin Buohara told a news conference.
The two largest possessors of chemical weapons have both signed the treaty prohibiting the development, production or use of chemical weapons but have yet to ratify it.
The Preparatory Commision for the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) has said their ratification was crucial for its success.

The convention will enter into force on April 29, 1997 after Hungary became the 65th country to ratify it on Thursday. Under the terms of the accord, it becomes active 180 days after the receipt by the United Nations of the 65th ratification.

The convention, which is of unlimited duration, has so far been signed by 160 countries including all five permanent members of the Security Council -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France. But among them only Britain and France have so far ratified the accord.
The U.S. Senate decided in June to vote on ratification by September 14. Russia is expected to follow suit.

"I would like to call on all countries to exercise greater political will and urgency to resolve outstanding issues now the trigger point has been reached. There is now no turning back," Buohara said.
Now that the trigger of 65 ratifications has been reached, the OPCW will take on up to 200 inspectors to monitor compliance with the convention's tough verification measures.
Signatories must destroy their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide detailed information about the production and export of listed chemicals used to make such weapons.

They are barred from supplying listed chemicals to non-signatories -- such as Iraq, Libya, North Korea and Syria -- and must open their chemical plants to the OPCW both for routine and short-notice challenge inspections.
The Dutch government welcomed the activation of the convention. "It is a milestone in the history of arms control and disarmament," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"Through this will come hopefully, 82 years after the first chemical weapons were used at Ypres, in Belgium, during the First World War, a definite end to the threat of these gruesome weapons," the statement said.
The convention is the first disarmament agreement negotiated in a multilateral framework that provides for the elimination of an entire category of weapons of mass destruction.
